comments.author: fedupwithbadair
comments.text:
I'm a computer scientist who has been doing clean-air advocacy on a regular basis for over six years now.  Based on what I have read in the scientific journals and news outlets and the experts and other advocates I have spoken with, I think there are three major issues relating to legislation and regulation of ultrafine particles (UFPs).

First, most G7 nations (not Canada, because fortunately we take science seriously in this country) take an AAQS (ambient air quality standards) approach to the issue of air pollution.  This is extremely dangerous and fallacious because it relies on picking an arbitrary risk level and setting standards to align with that, instead of acknowledging the basic scientific fact that there is no safe level of air pollution (above zero) (see e.g. https://www1.racgp.org.au/newsgp/clinical/there-s-no-safe-level-of-air-pollution) and acting accordingly.  Because no two people respond exactly the same way to a given dose and composition of air pollution, this risk-based approach is unfair and a form of inequality and environmental injustice.

Second, UFPs don't just get into the bloodstream - they are so small that they are able to penetrate cells' membranes and the toxins they carry directly damage the cells' DNA (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/11/231114143839.htm).  It only takes one cancerous cell to spark that proverbial wildfire.

Third, for some sources of pollution (especially, it seems, diesel engines and wood-burning appliances - see https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/improved-cookstoves-emit-more-ultrafine-particles-conventional-stoves), it seems like the "cleaner" the combustion is, the more UFPs that are emitted from it.  It may seem counterintuitive, but it's true.

We need to stop treating air pollution as a threshold issue and pivot to tackling every source of it that we can, because the only way we're going to win the UFP battle is to not produce them in the first place - because once you generate them, it's too late.  There is no way to filter them because they just slip right through as if the filter isn't even there.

Thank you to the CBC for opening this discussion for debate and insight.

And yes you are correct about HEPA filters. These high efficiency filters are designed to catch tiny particles like ultrafine particles versus the standard home purifier which is only able to filter particles much larger than UFPs. All HEPA filters have a rating of a MERV 17 or higher and will trap 99.9% of air particles that are 0.1-1.0 micron size. HEPA filters will definitely remove ultra fines. But you need to get one that's big enough to handle the space. So for some of these units that might be multiple, you might need one in the bedroom and one in the lliving room. comments.author: Exan Auyoung
comments.text:
Hi Thierry, 
Experts recommend HEPA or MERV filters. Although it’s costly, these high efficiency filters are designed to catch tiny particles like ultrafine particles versus the standard home purifier which is only able to filter particles that are larger than UFPs. All HEPA filters have a rating of a MERV 17 or higher and will trap 99.9% of air particles that are 0.1-1.0 micron size.  HEPA filters will definitely remove ultra fines particles. But you need to get one that's big enough to handle the space. So for some of these units that might be multiple, you might need one in the bedroom and one in the living room.  Although UFPs have been linked to some illnesses including cardiovascular, dementia, respiratory illnesses and lung cancer, it's difficult to say with certainty whether one individual's illness is caused by UFPS with complete certainty. That's because there are a variety of factors that could be contributing to one person's illness. As Scott Weichenthal, one of the experts in our story said "For people who are experiencing things like asthma or COPD or dementia, those things are certainly consistent with what we know about the health effects of these particles. But we certainly can't say that definitively that's why they got these things.” However, there is a growing body of evidence that shows UFPs do have an impact on our health so experts like Weichenthal are calling for regulation.

And people are paying the price.

Canadians are already dealing with record levels of anxiety, isolation, and depression. Constant warnings about invisible threats push vulnerable people further into withdrawal, avoidance, and distress. This isn’t a side effect—it’s a predictable outcome.

Of course, public health matters. But so does mental health. When messaging becomes relentless and worst-case focused, it stops helping and starts harming.

At some point, we have to ask: are we informing people, or are we scaring them?

Right now, it feels like the latter.
